steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for an NLP paper about temporal misalignment in open-retrieval question answering. The idea is to predict how long facts stay true and abstain from answers that are likely outdated; cover the problem, why existing fixes fall short, our new task, and how we evaluate it.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Problem: temporal misalignment in deployed NLP systems
- Why existing fixes (model editing, retrieval) are incomplete
- Our proposal: fact duration prediction, abstain on outdated facts
- Intrinsic and extrinsic evaluations
- Other applications in QA; summary

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Problem: temporal misalignment
  - model trained on past data, evaluated on present data
  - performance degradation across many NLP tasks
  - esp. knowledge-intensive tasks, e.g. open-retrieval QA; world knowledge changes rapidly
  - shift toward large pretrained models: too expensive to retrain, recite outdated facts
- Existing fixes
  - update knowledge stored in parameters of pretrained model
  - retrieval-based systems: non-parametric corpus of facts, updatable over time
  - both incomplete: need an oracle to identify which facts to update + continuous curation of up-to-date corpus
- Our proposal
  - abstain from presenting facts predicted to be out of date
  - new task: fact duration prediction (how frequently a fact changes)
  - classification and regression-based baselines
  - distant supervision: fact durations from temporal knowledge bases; duration-related news text
  - discussion: relation to temporal commonsense
- Evaluations
  - intrinsic: how close duration estimates are to ground truth
    - distant supervision only: 65% of temporally dependent facts (real search queries, NaturalQuestions) within 3 years vs 11% for average-duration baseline
  - extrinsic: improving open-retrieval QA predictions under misalignment
    - main focus: calibration (Figure 1)
    - expected calibration error down 50-60% vs system confidence alone; two QA systems; SituatedQA
- Other applications
  - adaptive inference in ensembled open/closed-book QA: decide when retrieval is needed
  - retrieval over heterogeneous corpus (outdated + recent articles): relevance vs recency
  - first focused study on mitigating temporal misalignment in QA via fact durations

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
One of the core challenges when deploying NLP systems is temporal misalignment. This is when a model is trained on data that was collected in the past but is then evaluated on data from the present. Temporal misalignment makes performance degrade in many different NLP tasks. It is especially a problem for knowledge-intensive tasks like open-retrieval question answering (QA), because there the models have to make predictions based on world knowledge, and world knowledge can change quickly. The problem also gets worse as the way NLP systems are built keeps moving toward relying on large pretrained models, which are very expensive to retrain and which tend to recite outdated facts.

Prior work has tried to fix this by updating the knowledge that is stored in the parameters of an existing pretrained model. Other work has proposed retrieval-based systems that use a non-parametric corpus of facts, and this corpus can be updated over time. But both of these methods are incomplete solutions, since they rely on an oracle to tell which facts need to be updated and to keep curating a corpus of up-to-date facts.

Since it is hard to keep existing models up-to-date, we propose a different solution, where we abstain from presenting facts that we predict are out of date. To do this, we introduce fact duration prediction, which is the task of predicting how often a given fact changes, and we establish several baselines based on classification and regression. We also look at large-scale sources of distant supervision for the task, including fact durations extracted from temporal knowledge bases and news text that is related to durations. We discuss this challenging task in detail and explore how fact duration prediction relates to temporal commonsense.

- Evaluations
  - intrinsic: how close duration estimates are to ground truth
    - distant supervision only: 65% of temporally dependent facts (real search queries, NaturalQuestions) within 3 years vs 11% for average-duration baseline
  - extrinsic: improving open-retrieval QA predictions under misalignment
    - main focus: calibration (Figure 1)
    - expected calibration error down 50-60% vs system confidence alone; two QA systems; SituatedQA
- Other applications
  - adaptive inference in ensembled open/closed-book QA: decide when retrieval is needed
  - retrieval over heterogeneous corpus (outdated + recent articles): relevance vs recency
  - first focused study on mitigating temporal misalignment in QA via fact durations

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
One of the core challenges when deploying NLP systems is temporal misalignment. This is when a model is trained on data that was collected in the past but is then evaluated on data from the present. Temporal misalignment makes performance degrade in many different NLP tasks. It is especially a problem for knowledge-intensive tasks like open-retrieval question answering (QA), because there the models have to make predictions based on world knowledge, and world knowledge can change quickly. The problem also gets worse as the way NLP systems are built keeps moving toward relying on large pretrained models, which are very expensive to retrain and which tend to recite outdated facts.

Prior work has tried to fix this by updating the knowledge that is stored in the parameters of an existing pretrained model. Other work has proposed retrieval-based systems that use a non-parametric corpus of facts, and this corpus can be updated over time. But both of these methods are incomplete solutions, since they rely on an oracle to tell which facts need to be updated and to keep curating a corpus of up-to-date facts.

Since it is hard to keep existing models up-to-date, we propose a different solution, where we abstain from presenting facts that we predict are out of date. To do this, we introduce fact duration prediction, which is the task of predicting how often a given fact changes, and we establish several baselines based on classification and regression. We also look at large-scale sources of distant supervision for the task, including fact durations extracted from temporal knowledge bases and news text that is related to durations. We discuss this challenging task in detail and explore how fact duration prediction relates to temporal commonsense.

We evaluate our fact duration prediction systems in two ways. First, for intrinsic evaluation, we report how close the duration estimates of our systems are to the ground truth labels. We find that models trained only with distant supervision can predict the duration of 65% of temporally dependent facts from real search queries in NaturalQuestions to within 3 years, while a simple baseline that uses the average duration gets 11%. Second, for extrinsic evaluation, we measure how the duration estimates of the systems can improve the predictions of an open-retrieval QA system under temporal misalignment. We mostly focus on improving calibration (as shown in Figure 1). Our approach can reduce expected calibration error by 50-60% compared to using system confidence alone, on two QA systems on the SituatedQA dataset.

Finally, we also look at other ways to apply our fact duration systems in QA. We experiment with adaptive inference in ensembled open/closed-book QA systems, where we use duration prediction to decide when retrieval is needed because of temporal misalignment. We also apply fact duration prediction to a setting where retrieval is done over a heterogeneous corpus that has both outdated and recent articles, so the systems have to weigh how relevant an article is against how recent it is. Overall, we present the first focused study on mitigating temporal misalignment in QA by estimating the duration of facts.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
A core challenge in deploying NLP systems is managing temporal misalignment, where a model that is trained on data collected in the past is evaluated on data from the present [1]. Temporal misalignment causes performance degradation in a variety of NLP tasks [2,3,4]. This is especially true for knowledge-intensive tasks, such as open-retrieval question answering (QA) [5], where models must make predictions based on world knowledge that can change rapidly. Such issues are further exacerbated as the paradigm for creating NLP systems shifts toward relying on large pretrained models [6,7] that are prohibitively expensive to retrain and prone to reciting outdated facts.

Prior work has attempted to address these issues by updating the knowledge stored within the parameters of an existing pretrained model [8,9,10]. Another line of work has proposed retrieval-based systems, which use a non-parametric corpus of facts that can be updated over time [11,12,13]. Both methods, however, are incomplete solutions, as they rely on an oracle to identify which facts need to be updated and to continuously curate a corpus of up-to-date facts.

Given the difficulty of keeping existing models up-to-date, we propose an alternative solution in which we abstain from presenting facts that we predict are out of date. To accomplish this, we introduce fact duration prediction, the task of predicting how frequently a given fact changes, and establish several classification and regression-based baselines. We also explore large-scale sources of distant supervision for this task, including fact durations extracted from temporal knowledge bases [14] and duration-related news text [15]. We discuss this challenging task in depth, exploring the relationship between fact duration prediction and temporal commonsense [16].

We provide two sets of evaluations for our fact duration prediction systems. First, as intrinsic evaluations, we report how close our systems' duration estimates are to ground truth labels. We find that models trained with only distant supervision can predict the duration of 65% of temporally dependent facts from real search queries in NaturalQuestions [17] to within 3 years, compared to 11% for a simple average-duration baseline. Second, in extrinsic evaluations, we measure how our duration estimates can improve an open-retrieval QA system's predictions under temporal misalignment, focusing mainly on calibration (as depicted in Figure 1). Our approach reduces expected calibration error by 50-60% over using system confidence alone on two QA systems [18,11] on the SituatedQA dataset [4].

Lastly, we explore other ways of applying our fact duration systems in QA. We experiment with adaptive inference in ensembled open/closed-book QA systems, using duration prediction to decide when retrieval is necessary due to temporal misalignment. We also apply fact duration prediction in a scenario where retrieval is performed over a heterogeneous corpus containing both outdated and recent articles, and systems must weigh an article's relevance against its recency. In sum, we present the first focused study on mitigating temporal misalignment in QA through estimating the duration of facts.
